case_name: Kootenay Sleds & Wheels Inc. v. Peace Hills General Insurance Company
text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Kootenay Sleds & Wheels Inc. v.
Peace Hills General Insurance Company,

2012 BCSC 1504

Date: 20121012

Docket:
S95171

Registry: Kelowna

Between:

Kootenay
Sleds & Wheels Inc.

Plaintiff

And

Peace
Hills General Insurance Company and

Economical Mutual Insurance Company

Defendants

And

Kootenay
Sleds & Wheels Inc.,

B.S. Contracting Ltd., Bruce Streichert and

Jaynee Streichert

Defendants by Counterclaim

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice Betton

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Plaintiff: and the

Defendants by Counterclaim:

J.G.
Hardwick

Counsel for the Defendants:

N.P.
Kent

Place and Date of Hearing:

Kelowna,
B.C.

July
4, 2012

Place and Date of Judgment:

Kelowna,
B.C.

October
12, 2012

Introduction

[
1
]

The applicants, Peace Hills General Insurance
Company and Economical Mutual Insurance Company, are the defendants in this
action. They seek an order that the plaintiff, Kootenay Sleds & Wheels
Inc., (“KSW”) pay security for the costs it may be liable to pay to the
applicants if it is unsuccessful in its claim. In addition it asks that there
be a stay of these proceedings until that security is given.

[
2
]

KSW’s claim is for a declaration that the
defendants are required to pay KSW’s claim for fire losses under a policy of
insurance issued by the defendants. That fire loss occurred on December 31,
2008.

Background

[
3
]

KSW was in the business of selling and servicing
recreational vehicles in Nelson, British Columbia. It operated out of two
buildings; generally one was used for sales and the other for service.

[
4
]

The principal of KSW, Bruce Streichert, bought
the shares of KSW from the Seminoffs in 2003.

[
5
]

At the time of the fire the Seminoffs continued
to be owners of the sales building and the associated property. Since 2005
there has been an ongoing dispute that is being litigated regarding a lease
purchase arrangement between KSW and the Seminoffs in respect of that building.

[
6
]

KSW’s business was conducted using inventory
financing from General Electric Commercial Distribution Finance Canada (“GE”).
In November 2008 GE gave notice that it was terminating the financing
arrangements effective February 4, 2009. While there is some issue on the
subject, Mr. Streichert maintains that he had communicated with GE
representatives regarding that notice. The plaintiff had not informed the
defendants of the fact of having received the notice as of the date of loss.

[
7
]

The policy of insurance was in place and effective
as of September 2008. The policy included the following conditions:

MATERIAL CHANGE

4.         Any change material to the risk
and within the control and knowledge of the Insured avoids the contract as to
the part affected thereby, unless the change is promptly notified in writing to
the Insurer or its local agent, ...

FRAUD

7.         Any
fraud or wilfully false statement in a statutory declaration in relation to any
of the above particulars [to be set out in the proof of loss], vitiates the
claim of the person making the declaration.

[
8
]

The policy also included terms that required the
defendants to pay GE the amount of its loss irrespective of any default by the
insured, the plaintiff. GE’s claim, based on those terms of the policy, has
been paid and that fact gives rise to the outstanding counterclaim against the
plaintiff. In its argument the defence says that the counterclaim serves two
functions:

•

In the event the plaintiff’s claim is dismissed,
it will result in a judgment against the defendants by counterclaim for the
approximate $1,000,000 claimed; and

•

In the event the plaintiff’s claim succeeds,
then the amounts paid to GE under the policy will be credited towards and
set-off against the amounts otherwise payable to KSW

[
9
]

The plaintiff retained an insurance adjuster to
assist in the preparation and submission of the plaintiff’s proofs of loss.

[
10
]

Included in the claims being made by the
plaintiff is a business interruption claim in excess of $400,000. That claim
seeks recovery for projected losses on a “business as usual” basis. In
addition, the plaintiff claims the loss of the sales building in the amount of
$389,182.

[
11
]

It is conceded by KSW that it is now insolvent.

[
12
]

The action was commenced December 16, 2009 and
the statement of defence was filed May 20, 2010. There have been numerous steps
and actions taken by both the plaintiff and the defendants in respect of the
claim to date.

Law

[
13
]

Section 236
of the
Business Corporations Act
,
S.B.C. 2002, c. 57 says:

If a corporation
is the plaintiff in a legal proceeding brought before the court, and if it
appears that the corporation will be unable to pay the costs of the defendant
if the defendant is successful in the defence, the court may require security
to be given by the corporation for those costs, and may stay all legal proceedings
until the security is given.

[
14
]

In
Kropp v. Swaneset Bay Golf Course Ltd.

(1997),
1997 CanLII 4037 (BC CA)
, 90 B.C.A.C. 170, the B.C. Court of Appeal endorsed a list of principles
as articulated in the English Court of Appeal, applicable to similar English
legislation. In noting them to be “a useful guide to the application of
s. 229 [now
s. 236
]”, they are summarized as follows:

1.         The
court has a complete discretion whether to order security, and will act in
light of all the relevant circumstances;

2.         The
possibility or probability that the plaintiff company will be deterred from
pursuing its claim is not without more sufficient reason for not ordering
security;

3.         The
court must attempt to balance injustices arising from use of security as an
instrument of oppression to stifle a legitimate claim on the one hand, and use
of impecuniosity as a means of putting unfair pressure on a defendant on the
other;

4.         The
court may have regard to the merits of the action, but should avoid going into
detail on the merits unless success or failure appears obvious;

5.         The
court can order any amount of security up to the full amount claimed, as long
as the amount is more than nominal;

6.         Before
the court refuses to order security on the ground that it would unfairly stifle
a valid claim, the court must be satisfied that, in all the circumstances, it
is probable that the claim would be stifled; and

7.         The lateness
of the application for security is a circumstance which can properly be taken
into account.

[
15
]

More recently, the B.C. Court of Appeal again
addressed the issues in
Galaxy Sports Inc. v. Umbro Holdings Ltd.
,
2004
BCCA 208
. There it again affirmed the above-noted list of relevant
considerations as set out in
Kropp
. In doing so it noted in paragraphs
16 and 17 as follows:

[16]      ... The Court stated that, in
order to show that an order for security for costs would stifle its action, the
corporate plaintiff had to do more than simply state that it was impecunious;
it had to lead evidence indicating that it had no means of raising money for
security. ...

[17]      In my view, the
Kropp

decision does not stand for the proposition that
full
security for costs
must be ordered where the company resisting the posting of security fails to
lead adequate evidence concerning its ability to obtain financial assistance
from third parties. Failure to lead such evidence may well result in an order
for security for costs, but the
amount
of security lies within the
discretion of the chambers judge to be exercised having regard to a variety of
considerations. ...

(emphasis in original)

[
16
]

In
Scotford Electrical & Technical
Services Ltd. v. Blue Mountain Log Sales Ltd.
,
2005 BCSC 538
, Master Groves
(as he then was) quoted Romilly J. in
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc.
v. Canadian Jewish Congress
(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4th) 266 (B.C.S.C.) as
follows:

[13]      Romilly J. set out in ¶ 14 the
following process to be followed in an application under what is now s. 236
of the
Act
:

14        Based
then, on the decision in
Kropp
, supra
as well as the
decision of Spencer J. in
Ruko
, supra
, the test to be
applied on an application for security for costs is as follows:

1.         Does it
appear that the plaintiff company will be unable to pay the defendants' costs
if the action fails?

2.         If so,
has the plaintiff shown that it has exigible assets of sufficient value to
satisfy an award of costs?

3.         Is the
court satisfied that the defendants have an arguable defence to present?

4.         Would
an order for costs visit undue hardship on the plaintiff such that it would
prevent the plaintiff's case from being heard?

[14]      The fourth question set out by
Romilly J. is where a court considers,
inter alia
, the possibility that
a claim will be stifled. Romilly J. made the following points on this question
at ¶’s 22-23:

22        To
succeed in showing that an order for security would stifle the action, the
plaintiff must show that it has insufficient assets and no means of raising
money for security:
Kropp
,
supra
. In the case at bar,
there is dearth evidence as to the financial state of affairs of the plaintiff.
There is also a dearth of evidence as to any access the plaintiff may have to
resources. Consequently, though it appears that the plaintiff may be unable to
pay costs of the action, it does not follow, in the absence of evidence, that
such a state of affairs would result in stifling the advancement of the
plaintiff's claim if costs were ordered to be secured.

23        In sum, on an application for
security for costs, once the defendants have established a
prima facie

case that the plaintiff lacks exigible assets, the plaintiff is required to
respond with evidence to establish either that it will be able to pay the defendants'
costs, that the defendants have no arguable case, or that an order for security
will stifle the action. These tests serve to balance the possible injustice of
stifling the corporate plaintiff's claim against the possible injustices of
exposing the defendants to a law suit where they could not recover their costs
if successful.

[
17
]

Reference is also made in paragraph 20 to
Apex Mountain Resort Ltd.
v. British Columbia
,
1998 CarswellBC 1758 (S.C.)
where Bauman J. (as he
then was) referred to the
Kropp
decision. Paragraphs 29 and 30 of
Apex

read as follows:

[29]      In
Kropp
, Finch J.A.
(at 315) specifically referred to the principles "as more fully
articulated and explained in
Keary
" as a useful guide in
British Columbia.

[30]      Looking at
Keary
,
then, we find this more complete exposition of principle 3 (at 540 of
Keary
):

The court must
carry out a balancing exercise. On the one hand it must weigh the injustice to
the plaintiff if prevented from pursuing a proper claim by an order for
security. Against that, it must weigh the injustice to the defendant if no
security is ordered and at the trial the plaintiff's claim fails and the
defendant finds himself unable to recover from the plaintiff the costs which
have been incurred by him in his defence of the claim.
The court will
properly be concerned not to allow the power to order security to be used as an
instrument of oppression, such as by stifling a genuine claim by an indigent
company against a more prosperous company, particularly when the failure to
meet that claim might in itself have been a material cause of the plaintiff's
impecuniosity
(see
Farrer v Lacy, Hartland & Co

(1885) 28
Ch D 482 at 485
per Bowen LJ). But it will also be concerned not to be so
reluctant to order security that it becomes a weapon whereby the impecunious
company can use its inability to pay costs as a means of putting unfair
pressure on the more prosperous company (see
Pearson v Naydler

[1977] 3 All ER 531 at 537, [1977] 1 WLR 899 at 906)
.

(emphasis
added by Bauman J.)

Analysis

[
18
]

There are some important facts which are not in dispute in this
application.

[
19
]

First, the plaintiff acknowledges that it is insolvent. In its argument
it notes that there is at least some connection between the fire loss, which is
the foundation of this action, and that current state of insolvency. It is a
logical connection, even in light of the notice that had been received by the
plaintiff from GE.

[
20
]

That notice was a looming problem for KSW. Mr. Streichert
was optimistic that the problem would be solved. It is not clear how that would
have resolved.

[
21
]

The fire and the defendants’ position with respect to
the resulting insurance claim made continuing in business impossible.

[
22
]

In addition the plaintiff acknowledges that the
defendants have an arguable defence. The defendants suggest that their defences
are much stronger than arguable. Clearly, based on
Kropp
,
it is not
appropriate to get into the merits of the action unless success or failure
appears obvious. On the evidence before me, I am not prepared to categorize the
result of this case as “obvious”.

[
23
]

The defendants agree that if the plaintiff’s claim is
stayed pending the posting of security, the counterclaim should also be stayed.

[
24
]

In his first affidavit Mr. Streichert, on behalf
of the plaintiff, says that KSW has exhausted its resources in pursuit of this
litigation and the litigation with the Seminoffs referenced above. He also
refers to the sale of property, the borrowing of funds from family, and taking
employment in the logging industry. His home is in foreclosure, and he and the
company are being pursued for outstanding debts through litigation. Paragraph
41 of his affidavit reads:

If an order for security for
costs is made against KSW in any amount more than nominal, I verily believe
that KSW will be barred from advancing its claims arising from the fire.

These statements are in support of the assertion that an
order for security will stifle the plaintiff’s claim as referenced in the third
and sixth enumerated considerations set out in
Kropp
above.

[
25
]

The defendants reference the decision in
Fat Mel’s Restaurant Ltd. v.
Canadian Northern Shield Insurance Co.
(1993),
1993 CanLII 1669 (BC CA)
, 25 B.C.A.C. 95. There at
paragraph 16 the court noted:

... However,
once the applicant for security has shown that the plaintiff will not be able
to pay costs should the claim fail, security is generally ordered unless the
court is satisfied that there is no arguable defence. ...

[
26
]

The plaintiff says that
Fat Mel’s
is no longer the law and it has
been overtaken by
Kropp
and
Galaxy
.

[
27
]

The court, in
Kropp
, referenced
Fat Mel’s
in its synopsis
of the defendant’s position. There the defendant was relying on
Fat Mel’s

for the same purpose as the defendants here. The court, in
Kropp
, then
noted at paragraph
14
:

There does not
appear to be any decision of this court setting out a complete statement of the
applicable principles, and relevant criteria, in exercising the court's
discretion under s. 229 of the
Company Act
. ...

It then goes on to consider the
Keary
decision
and endorses the principles set out in that decision, which I note post-dated
the decision in
Fat Mel’s
. I agree with the plaintiff that the
Kropp

and
Galaxy
decisions expand the analysis, and the inability of the
plaintiff to pay costs if unsuccessful and the existence of an arguable defence
are only part of the analysis.

[
28
]

The timing of an application of a security for costs is relevant. In
this case the plaintiff was already heavily invested in the action which was
more than two years old before the application for security for costs was
initiated.

[
29
]

The defendants, in the notice of application, set out the position that
security should be in excess of $200,000. This was based on a draft bill of
costs, using Scale C and already incurred and anticipated expert costs. In its
argument it suggested that the appropriate level of security would be $100,000.

[
30
]

The plaintiff says that there should be no security, or alternatively in
a reduced amount.

[
31
]

As has been noted in the authorities, this is a balancing exercise.
There is a link between the insolvency of the plaintiff and the substance of
the claim it advances. The application was initiated after the plaintiff was
heavily invested in the litigation. The plaintiff is, however, insolvent and
the defendants have arguable defences. If successful in those defences, the
defendants would not be able to recover against the plaintiff.

[
32
]

Balancing the considerations in the context of this case, it is my
conclusion that it is appropriate to make an order for security but in a
reduced amount. The appropriate amount is $40,000.

[
33
]

The claim and the counterclaim will be stayed, pending the posting of
adequate security in the amount of $40,000.

[
34
]

I have not heard from the parties with respect to costs of this
application.

“D.A.
Betton J.”

The Honourable Mr. Justice Betton
